# Full topics: compact domain → level → DAG

36,628 topics, exact names/levels/order retained. Each base-36 short ID is its 1-based position, not a graph ID. Level is inherited from the enclosing header. Teaching and assignment text used by these topics is embedded at the end of this file, keyed by short ID. Noise IDs in this pack's meta-rules remain reconciliation-only.

Level legend: H=HS; U=UG; J=UG+PG; P=PG-only; I=industry; ?=level-unknown (not reclassified).

# Embedded curriculum text

Each block below is copied verbatim from the original teaching source. The short IDs listed after Used by: are the compact topic IDs in this file that use the block. A lexical link is not a guarantee of complete teaching or assessment scope.

## Teaching blocks

### T0001

Used by: 24g, 29b, 2tt, 3hb, 4hp, 8f1, ays, bke, btc, btm, bv8, bvv, bx1, bx5, bxi, bye, bz9, c0e, c1h, c1s, c1v, c5y, c62, ciw, ckg, ckk, cs9, css, cvy, dbi, dgi, dhx, di9, dpg, dpj, dvk, dw7, fll, g16, gbx, hn7, jzv, k6u, mbl, mpf, mri, njn, nrk, p1z, p69, pr1, pre, prh, qk5, qq0

- **Topics:** Course introduction (Week 0): aims, structure, hands-on labs, assessment. *So, What's the Cloud anyway? Start with a Solid Platform.* Cloud basics, big data and machine learning, and where and how the Google Cloud Platform fits in. Cloud computing as on-demand delivery of computations, storage, applications and other IT resources through a cloud services platform over the internet with a pay-as-you-go business model. Why clouds, what is a cloud, what's new in today's clouds; cloud computing versus distributed computing; utility computing; features of today's clouds: massive scale. X-as-a-service (the source writes "AAS") classification: HaaS, IaaS, PaaS, SaaS. Data-intensive computing; new cloud paradigms. Categories of clouds: private clouds, public clouds (and hybrid, community, multi-cloud). History and evolution of cloud: time-sharing, clusters and grids, utility computing, virtualization, web services, hyperscale data centers. Types of cloud computing and who operates what in each service model. Outline map of the cloud-and-distributed-systems course (named topics and where taught): an in-depth understanding of distributed computing concepts, distributed algorithms and the techniques that underlie today's cloud computing technologies; virtualization (U4.2), cloud storage with key-value/NoSQL stores (U10.3 to U10.6), cloud networking (U4.4, U4.6, U4.8), fault-tolerance cloud using PAXOS (U9.14), peer-to-peer systems (U9.4, U9.5), classical distributed algorithms such as leader election (U9.10), time and ordering in distributed systems (U9.6), distributed mutual exclusion (U9.8), distributed algorithms for failures and recovery approaches (U9.19), emerging areas of big data (D11) and many others; industry systems such as Apache Spark (U11.4), Google's Chubby and Apache Zookeeper (U9.15), HBase (U10.5), MapReduce (U11.3), Apache Cassandra (U10.4), Google's B4 and Microsoft's Swan (U4.6), and the intimate knowledge of the internals of cloud computing and of how distributed-systems concepts work inside clouds that the course promises.

### T0002

Used by: 5ok

- **Results:** Statistical-multiplexing economy: for n independent demands with mean μ and standard deviation σ, pooled capacity μn + kσ√n versus n(μ + kσ) when dedicated, so the saving per tenant grows like σk(1 − 1/√n) [D]. Break-even utilisation between on-demand and owned capacity (cost per used hour = price ÷ utilisation) [D]. Elasticity as a queueing statement: a fixed fleet is stable only while demand rate < capacity [D, from U2.1]. NIST essential characteristics are a definition [Def].

### T0003

Used by: 94d, cgc, mmi, n7t, nsi, ovi, ra8

- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: NIST SP 800-145; Armbrust 2010, recalled, not checked]* five essential characteristics (on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service), three service models, four deployment models; the shared-responsibility model (taught properly in U7.7); edge computing (taught in U4.4).

### T0004

Used by: n, q5, 4hz, 54r, 663, 68e, 6xo, axb, boa, bvp, bxn, cnl, e3b, eny, f20, fa3, fc6, fck, fp6, fpb, fti, g1t, g2r, g3j, g7r, ga7, ha5, jjj, l16, l19, lg1, lls, m0q, m0r, mbv, mey, muk, ngz, p6v, pt9

- **Topics:** Processes and file descriptors, pipes and redirection, exit status, signals, job control; shell grammar: quoting, parameter expansion, globbing, here-documents, functions, `set -euo pipefail`; the core toolbox (`find`, `grep`, `sed`, `awk`, `xargs`, `curl`, `ssh`, `scp`, `tar`); environment variables and secret hygiene (no secret in code, notes or history); regular expressions as regular languages: concatenation, union, Kleene star, NFA and DFA, Thompson construction, why `grep` matching is linear time; Python for systems work: bytes versus str, files, `subprocess`, `argparse`, `json`, virtual environments, threads versus `asyncio`; Git: the commit DAG, content-addressed objects, branches, three-way merge, `.gitignore` for secrets.

### T0005

Used by: 7m7

- **Build:** a regex engine (concatenation, `|`, `*`, `+`, `?`, classes) by Thompson NFA simulation, tested against `re`; a small shell that runs pipelines with `os.fork`, `os.pipe`, `os.dup2`, `os.execvp`. [local]

### T0006

Used by: lg7, qhv

- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface; Sipser Ch.1, recalled, not checked]* POSIX signals semantics, `trap`-based cleanup (used in teardown scripts), shellcheck as the linter.

### T0007

Used by: 222, 22q, 8y0, buz, c0a, c5x, cjw, erg, fob, g2n, g2s, g7l, ggl, l5m, lan, lsm, lv7, mj4, mrj, mrt, n3o, ne7, oc7, psg, psh, pue, ria

- **Topics:** Google Cloud Platform overview; core infrastructure; the resource hierarchy (organization, folders, projects), project name, ID and number; billing accounts, budgets and alerts; regions and zones; the Cloud Console, Cloud Shell and the `gcloud` grammar (`gcloud <group> <command> --flags`, `--format=json`, configurations); enabling APIs, quotas; a first look at IAM members, roles and policies (taught in U7.7); the 26 labs on Qwiklabs that are part of the course: lab protocol (temporary lab project and credentials, never a work account), cost tag per lab, budget alert before any paid resource, same-day teardown; free tier, credits and student programmes.

### T0008

Used by: cct

- **Results:** IAM policy inheritance down the hierarchy is a union of allows [Def]; per-second billing arithmetic and cost of an idle resource over a month [D]; teardown-first rule: every create has a recorded delete [Def].

### T0009

Used by: 5p4, m0h, m7l, mq0, ng0, qpg, qph

- **Gap-fills:** *[checked against press and Google pages this session]* Qwiklabs was acquired by Google in November 2016, became Google Cloud Skills Boost in October 2021 and is now part of Google Skills (announced October 2025), with a monthly free credit allowance that changes; the course's own lab list is not in the source (Appendix F). Product names change often (Stackdriver became the operations suite in 2020; Cloud AI Platform and AutoML became Vertex AI in 2021; AI Platform access ended 31 January 2025): verify names in the console before relying on them.

### T0010

Used by: 28, 2d, cz, of, 17x, 2ap, 2gs, 2kc, 2r6, 34r, 3ao, 4s2, 7db, 7gg, bvi, d0j, ev2, j4v, jg6, lla, m3p, nth

- **Topics:** Probability from first principles (sample spaces, conditional probability, Bayes' rule, random variables, expectation, variance, the standard distributions and the memoryless property) is taught once, in U21.6, and is entered from there; what networks add here is the Poisson process (three equivalent definitions, superposition, thinning); continuous-time Markov chains and birth–death chains; the M/M/1 queue: stationary distribution, mean number in system, mean delay, utilisation; Little's law; M/M/c and Erlang C; M/M/1/K and blocking; M/G/1 and the Pollaczek–Khinchine formula; bandwidth–delay product as the "pipe" volume.

### T0011

Used by: 2k, af, 4bp, 8ke, od6, od7

- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Kleinrock; Bertsekas–Gallager; recalled, not checked]* PASTA (statement), Jackson networks (statement), heavy-tail traffic and self-similarity as a caveat to Poisson models. The probability itself is taught from first principles in U21.6 and as statistics in U19.3.

### T0012

Used by: 25x, 3os, 4bc, 7h2, 91y, aa6, bw6, bz1, c0b, c2a, c3i, dcz, dps, dzj, e3y, eje, fda, gnf, ipj, ist, isy, itb, iyw, j7b, j7k, j94, jka, jm9, knk, nhq, nsk, ntf, oad, okv, pn7, q1e, q9m, qfb, qjm, rbo, ric

- **Topics:** Objectives: (i) architecture and principles of today's computer networks, (ii) protocols and their functionalities, (iii) requirements for the future Internet and its impact on network architecture; growth of the Internet from traditional circuit-switched and packet-switched small-scale networks to modern high-speed mobile and wireless Internet; methods, architectures and designs at every protocol level for a secure and highly dependable information technology infrastructure; the top-down approach. *Introduction to Computer Networks History:* ARPANET, packet switching (Baran, Davies, Kleinrock), TCP/IP adoption, NSFNET, the Web. Network edge, access networks and the core. *Circuit Switching and Packet Switching:* FDM and TDM circuits, store-and-forward packet switching, statistical multiplexing, datagram versus virtual-circuit service. Delays: nodal processing, queuing, transmission and propagation; loss; throughput and bottleneck links; bandwidth–delay product; traceroute as a delay probe. Outline map of the networks course: a top-down approach covering the different protocols of the TCP/IP protocol stack, and touching on the next generation computer networks (the future Internet, U2.14 and D3), where a large number of methods are surveyed and the broad objective is to understand how the layers fit together.

### T0013

Used by: 3ra, 6zi, 86e, 8ln, bkb, ebv, pa8, rf2

- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Kurose–Ross Ch.1; Peterson–Davie Ch.1]* access technologies (DSL, cable, fibre, cellular, Wi-Fi), protocol layering preview, brief network-security threat overview (taught in D6).

### T0014

Used by: 2a7, 7mz, bwp, c0t, e8x, eln, eq3, eti, exc, g2x, gp7, hmq, ipc, j9b, koo, l4s, mmn, nl6, nl9, q7f, q95, rg5

- **Topics:** TCP/IP protocol stack, basic overview: application, transport, network, link and physical layers; comparison with the OSI reference model; protocols, services, interfaces and service access points; encapsulation and decapsulation of protocol data units; header formats for Ethernet, IPv4, UDP and TCP; port numbers and the socket API; network byte order. Introduction to ethical hacking: what it is, scope, legality and rules of engagement (developed in U6.1). Fundamentals of computer networking; TCP/IP protocol stack.

### T0015

Used by: j9h

- **Results:** Layering as information hiding with a cost: header overhead arithmetic for a TCP/IPv4/Ethernet stack [D]; the Internet checksum (one's-complement sum) is independent of byte order and can be updated incrementally [P]; a socket pair identifies a connection [Def].

### T0016

Used by: bet

- **Build:** an encoder and decoder for Ethernet, IPv4, UDP, TCP and ICMP headers with `struct`; the Internet checksum; a synthetic-capture writer and a pcap-style reader; loopback echo servers over TCP and UDP. Then Wireshark or `tcpdump` on loopback as the professional tool, naming what it decodes that the toy did not. [local]

### T0017

Used by: q1i

- **Gap-fills:** *[inferred: Stevens, TCP/IP Illustrated; Tanenbaum]* OSI versus Internet critique, socket options, loopback and namespaces for lab isolation (used from U2.12).

### T0018

Used by: 3xv, 64f, 7nd, 844, aqi, b2i, bfw, bka, blh, bwo, dix, e77, e9p, eal, ej8, emr, euj, ezz, fde, fk8, jf0, jim, ld7, lm0, mlk, mvo, n34, n47, okw, p3z, pnc, qy5

- **Topics:** Application layer services. HTTP: request and response format, methods, status codes, persistent connections and pipelining (HTTP/1.1), cookies, web caching with conditional GET, proxies; HTTP/2 multiplexing and HTTP/3 over QUIC. FTP: separate control and data connections, active versus passive mode. Email: SMTP, POP3, IMAP, MIME. DNS: hierarchy of root, TLD and authoritative servers, recursive versus iterative resolution, resource records (A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, MX, TXT), caching and TTL, message format. Client–server versus peer-to-peer architectures; the socket programming interface. The engineering use of DNS (managed services, traffic routing, trade-offs) is in U16.9.

### T0019

Used by: bk8

- **Results:** Page-load time model: non-persistent costs 2 RTT per object plus transmission, persistent with pipelining about one RTT for all objects [D]; cache hit-rate effect on average delay and on access-link utilisation [D]; DNS iterative resolution cost in RTTs with and without caching [D].

### T0020

Used by: lm7, mvj, ov9, ova

### T0099

Used by: 2f3, 2re, 2v4, 3ck, 3m6, 4yw, 5ib, 67h, 78l, 7mx, 82l, 8hx, 91q, 9by, bad, bx3, c2e, ejb, fih, fx5, gee, gn8, gnk, goe, gqu, gsc, gss, gun, gw4, gw9, h08, h19, h1b, h24, h2t, h3z, hag, hd0, irn, jh7, kja, l1b, l9e, lc3, lr7, lxu, m1z, m6y, mvs, n2q, ngu, osi, ous, ovb, ovj, oxj, p7v, psv, ptj, pvh, qij, r1p

- **Topics:** Introduction to cryptography: goals (confidentiality, integrity, authentication, non-repudiation), Kerckhoffs' principle, attacker models (ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext, chosen-ciphertext). Classical cryptosystems: shift, affine, monoalphabetic and polyalphabetic ciphers (Vigenère, autokey, Playfair, Hill), transposition. More on classical cryptosystems and various analysis: frequency analysis, index of coincidence, Kasiski examination, Friedman's test. Symmetric key cryptography and symmetric-key encryption (Gen, Enc, Dec); historical ciphers; private-key encryption and public-key encryption introduced (Ethical Hacking Week 6). Perfect security and its limitations: Shannon's theorem, the one-time pad, the key-length barrier. Course overview. Outline map of the cryptography courses (named topics and where taught): block and stream ciphers (U5.4, U5.6, U5.7), elliptic curve cryptography (U5.15), zero-knowledge proofs (U5.24), homomorphic encryption (U5.23), identity-based, attribute-based and functional encryption (U5.22), two-party and multi-party computation (U5.21), bitcoin and crypto-currency (U9.21), post-quantum cryptography (U5.25); real-world applications in secure communications and digital payments (the channel of U13.2, the signatures of U5.17 and the blockchain of U9.21); the evolving landscape of cyber threats and the cybersecurity challenges the cryptanalysis part addresses: network security, data security, mobile security, cloud security (U7.7) and endpoint security (U6.4); careers in cybersecurity, software engineering and digital forensics (evidence handling in U8.4); the aim of the provable-security course to let you read current research papers and standards.

### T0100

Used by: h6c

- **Results:** Shannon's theorem: for |M| = |K| = |C| a scheme is perfectly secret iff keys are uniform and each (m, c) pair has exactly one key [P]; perfect secrecy forces |K| ≥ |M| [P]; the one-time pad is perfectly secret and two-time pad reveals m₁ ⊕ m₂ [P]; the index of coincidence is about 0.066 for English and 1/26 for uniform text, which gives the Vigenère key length [D]; the affine cipher key space is φ(26)·26 = 312 [D].

### T0114

Used by: 4qp, gnu, gr8, gyl, gz4, l28, lov, lz3, mho, mnr, n4e, n4m, of2, oux, ovx, qaj, qn8, qn9, s3o

Used by: 1dp, 237, 287, 4cj, 4cm, 4ez, 4j1, 4ku, 76m, 9o9, gm2, gug, gxl, h1k, h6n, h92, h9r, h9t, j0s, l5y, lhw, lut, lva, lvb, m5t, nh4, o9k, o9y, o9z, oa7, odw, ohz, pfi, qzd, qze, qzf

### T0117

Used by: 607, 85e, 86o, bfu, bfv, db6, g9j, go4, h00, h8h, h8n, hbm, hd2, l2k, lav, n8f, ndi, nt6, o2q, ofm, p20, p7c, pw9, r3s, r4l

### T0118

Used by: h9w

- **Results:** A one-time MAC from a pairwise-independent family has forgery probability 1/p, so it is information-theoretically secure, and it cannot be reused [P]; a PRF is a secure fixed-length MAC with forgery advantage at most q/2ⁿ plus the PRF advantage [P]; plain CBC-MAC is forgeable on variable-length messages by a three-query splice [D]; encrypt-then-MAC with independent keys is CCA-secure when the cipher is CPA-secure and the MAC is strongly unforgeable [P]; HMAC security from the compression function as a PRF [X, beyond course scope].

- **Topics:** Digital signature: syntax and the existential-unforgeability game (EUF-CMA); forgeries on textbook RSA signatures and the hash-and-sign remedy (full-domain hash, PSS idea); RSA signatures; the Schnorr Identification Scheme (the interactive protocol itself is proved in U5.24) and Schnorr Signature by Fiat–Shamir; Digital Signature Standard (DSS): the DSA algorithm, ECDSA over the U5.15 curves, the role of the per-signature nonce, and EdDSA/Ed25519 with deterministic nonces; digital signatures in the TPMC Week 9 sense: group signature (anonymity within a group, traceable by a manager) and ring signature (ad hoc anonymity, no manager); one-time signatures from one-way functions (Lamport) and Merkle trees to many-time signatures, as a bridge to U5.25.

### T0135

### T0149

Used by: 23z, 25n, 26w, 4tz, 6cq, 7na, 8lk, bwj, d33, eh3, fb4, fs9, go2, goa, gx5, h0n, l5z, l7i, llr, n96, nvw, nvx, nwe, o1b, odt, of3, ohl, ohm, omr, ow7, oyx, p7x, po9, q6k, r9s, rlp, rlq, rls

### T0152

Used by: 2ju, 2nh, 37k, 3fm, 7a8, 7c4, 7lc, 91p, f8j, gs1, hbn, iai, ikt, jcr, k5m, kdo, l3f, l98, lgd, lid, mjt, mm2, mnf, mni, mvt, n4v, na0, nc1, nd8, nf1, ngq, oqy, oro, ov5, ow3, p15, p16, p1a, pcv, qih, qm7, qm8, r7a, r7c, rkd

- **Topics:** Introduction to quantum cryptography: qubits, measurement, no-cloning and the BB84 key-distribution protocol with its eavesdropping signature, reconciliation and privacy amplification; Shor's algorithm (period finding by the quantum Fourier transform and the classical reduction from factoring, and the discrete-log analogue) and Grover's algorithm (quadratic speed-up, hence doubling symmetric key length and hash output); post-quantum cryptography: lattice problems (SVP, LWE and module-LWE), Regev encryption, ring and module structure with the number-theoretic transform, the standardised ML-KEM and ML-DSA, hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA, building on U5.17), code-based (McEliece, and the selected HQC), multivariate and isogeny families and their break history (Rainbow and SIKE fell, from the primary papers), migration strategy (hybrid key exchange, crypto-agility, "harvest now, decrypt later"). As of this curriculum's date (November 2026), NIST published FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) on 13 August 2024, selected HQC for standardisation on 11 March 2025, and lists FN-DSA (FIPS 206) as still in development on its project page, checked on the web while building this curriculum. The source course names blockchain and bitcoin in the same final week; those are taught in U9.21 where consensus is available.

Outline map of the ethical-hacking course: starting from the basic topics of networking, network security and cryptography (D2, D5), with hands-on demonstrations that participants are encouraged to replicate, which in this curriculum happens only inside your own isolated laboratory.

Outline map (the named topics of the course outlines and where this curriculum teaches them): distributed hash tables (U9.5), the Google File System and HDFS (U10.2), Spark (U11.4), vector clocks (U9.6), distributed leader election (U9.10), the FLP result (U9.12), the CAP theorem (U9.16), commit protocols (U9.18), Bitcoin and blockchains (U9.21), distributed file systems (U10.2), and distributed programming languages, treated here: the actor model (Erlang and Akka style), communicating-sequential-process channels, remote procedure call and dataflow languages, with a small actor runtime built on DSim as the exercise. The common goal of the components in a distributed application, and the intimate knowledge of how things work in a distributed environment, are the stated outcomes.

- **Topics:** Outline map. The three source files are the NPTELSyllabus of the NOC course Fundamentals of Database Systems (a video course), the NPTEL Syllabus of Database Design (a video course) and the Introduction to Database Systems course of Prof. Sreenivasa Kumar, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, IIT Madras. They name these topics: databases at the core of digital systems and e-governance, the basics of database systems, the traditional relational systems and, briefly, the NoSQL paradigm used in big data systems (the Kanpur NOC course, sponsored by Aricent, with 48 lectures; here U15.27), the topics cover all important aspects including normalization, query processing and transactions (U15.11 to U15.13, U15.17, U15.18 and U15.20 to U15.23); the theoretical and practical principles involved in the design and use of databases systems with the help of a database management system (DBMS) and the SQL Standard, on which modern businesses and financial systems depend for their successful operation (the Madras course, with its Week plan from E/R Model to Transaction Processing: U15.2 to U15.23); and the eleven modules of Database Design from Introductory Concepts to Distributed databases (U15.1 to U15.26). Module 1, Introductory Concepts (1 session): Databases and Information Systems; An example usage context (a university: students, courses, instructors and enrolments, which is the running example of the whole domain); Database system concepts and architecture. Why a DBMS instead of files: redundancy and inconsistency, difficulty of access, isolation of data, integrity constraints, atomicity of updates, concurrent access, security. Data model, schema and instance; the three-schema architecture (external, conceptual and internal levels), logical and physical data independence; the data definition, data manipulation and query languages; database users (administrator, designers, application programmers, end users); the DBMS components (query processor with parser, optimiser and executor; storage manager with buffer manager, file manager, transaction manager, lock manager and recovery manager) and client/server and multi-tier deployment; online transaction processing against online analytical processing; a short history from hierarchical and network models through the relational model to object and NoSQL systems. Prerequisites stated by the sources (basic programming, data structures and algorithms; discrete mathematics): programming and data structures are assumed, and discrete mathematics is taught by the bridge U15.3 just before it is needed.

Relation schema, attribute, domain, tuple, relation instance, degree and cardinality; a relation is a set, so there is no tuple order and no duplicate; NULL and the three-valued logic it forces (taken up in U15.7); superkey, candidate key, primary key, alternate key; foreign keys and referential integrity; the constraints: domain, key, entity integrity and referential integrity; update operations insert, delete and update and what a DBMS does with a violation (reject, cascade, set NULL, set default). ER to relational mapping: strong entity, weak entity (owner key plus partial key), 1:1 (fold or merge), 1:N (foreign key on the N side), M:N (a relation of its own), multivalued attributes (a relation), n-ary relationships. The architecture, taught through the concepts this domain builds: a client connects to a database server; the engine runs agents (processes or threads) for each connection; the buffer pools cache pages of the table spaces, which are mapped to containers on disk; the log manager writes the write-ahead log; the lock manager and the cost-based optimiser sit between SQL and the access methods; the catalog holds the metadata. Data definition: CREATE TABLESPACE, BUFFERPOOL, TABLE (identity and generated columns), INDEX, VIEW and materialised query tables; data manipulation: standard SQL plus DB2 forms such as FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY and the one-row table SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1; the four isolation levels uncommitted read (UR), cursor stability (CS, the default), read stability (RS) and repeatable read (RR). The product family (Db2 for Linux, UNIX and Windows, Db2 for z/OS, Db2 for i) is named and the course case study follows the first.

A functional dependency X → Y as a constraint on every legal instance (a property of the schema, never of one instance); trivial and non-trivial dependencies; Armstrong's axioms (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) and the derived rules (union, decomposition, pseudotransitivity); the closure F⁺ of a set of dependencies and the attribute closure X⁺ with its algorithm; equivalence of dependency sets; the minimal (canonical) cover in three steps (single attribute on the right, remove extraneous attributes on the left, remove redundant dependencies); superkeys, candidate keys, prime and non-prime attributes, and finding all candidate keys; the insertion, deletion and update anomalies of U15.1 as the symptom of a bad dependency structure.

First normal form (atomic values, no repeating groups); second normal form (no non-prime attribute depends on part of a candidate key); third normal form (for every non-trivial X → A, X is a superkey or A is prime); Boyce–Codd normal form (for every non-trivial X → A, X is a superkey); the hierarchy BCNF inside 3NF inside 2NF inside 1NF. Decomposition: lossless join (the binary test), dependency preservation, projection of dependencies; the BCNF decomposition algorithm (which can lose dependencies) and the 3NF synthesis algorithm from a minimal cover (which is lossless and preserves dependencies); denormalisation for performance and for analytic stores (U12.2).

### T0298

Used by: 25l, 2hx, 4ia, 5gr, 5py, 67y, 6n3, ayp, biq, by5, dhy, luf, msr, nby, okp, pwk, pwl, q3c, qza, qzb, rgu, rlh

- **Topics:** Why the unit of cost changes: the memory hierarchy of U14.9 to U14.12 seen from the database, where a disk or flash access costs a million times a cache hit. The magnetic disk: platters, surfaces, tracks, cylinders, sectors, the head; the access time as seek plus rotational latency plus transfer; sequential against random access; the flash drive (pages, erase blocks, write amplification, no seek, asymmetric read and write cost); the block (page) as the unit of transfer. The external-memory (I/O) model of Aggarwal and Vitter with N records, a memory of M records and blocks of B records: scanning costs N/B transfers, sorting costs (N/B)·log_{M/B}(N/B) and a search in a block-indexed structure costs log_B N. External merge sort: run formation by sorting M records at a time or by replacement selection, then (M/B − 1)-way merges; double buffering to overlap transfer and computation.

### T0299

Used by: 4fc

- **Results:** The average rotational latency is half a revolution, 60/(2 × 7200) s = 4.17 ms at 7200 rpm, so a random 8 KB read with a 9 ms seek and a 150 MB/s transfer costs about 13.2 ms against 0.052 ms for the same block when it is the next one on the track [D, check]; external merge sort of N pages with M buffers takes 1 + ⌈log_{M−1}⌈N/M⌉⌉ passes, each reading and writing every page, so N = 10 000 and M = 100 give 3 passes and 60 000 page transfers [P, check by simulating the merge passes]; sorting needs Ω((N/B) log_{M/B}(N/B)) transfers, by counting: each transfer can distinguish only C(M, B) arrangements, and N! permutations must be told apart [S, the adversary argument is sketched, not written out]; replacement selection produces runs of average length about 2M on random input, by the snowplow argument [S, check: measured 1.99 M on 200 000 random keys]; a scan is the cheapest access and a random access the dearest, which is why the file organisations of U15.15 try to turn random into sequential access [D].

### T0372

Used by: 2r, hf, oi, ol, pn, 234, 2ad, 2b5, 2fo, 2h7, 2kf, 2ov, 2ri, 2st, 2u3, 2wg, 39c, 48e, 4ok, 4pp, 51e, 55a, 6yg, 7x6, 88w, 8yl, a8l, bvj, c4f, c4q, c4t, c8z, dq2, ezb, f77, f84, f92, fca, fh9, fub, g3s, hnx, i0g, i9x, iad, igb, izd, jyq, jys, k1l, k50, k5g, k87, kpg, kt5, l1g, l71, l94, l9x, lay, lck, ldv, lka, lkm, lln, lxf, lyt, lyv, mdz, mit, mj7, mjs, mk4, n69, o2i, o7l, omz, oqf, or3, or4, oxi, p5z, pll, qe2, qe3, qtp, qxp, rge, ris, rit

- **Topics:** the Bayesian course's stated prerequisite is R programming (it suggests the NPTEL course Foundations of R Software); this curriculum replaces R by Python throughout (decision of 2026-11-06), and this unit teaches what that prerequisite was for, in Python. The array: a flat buffer with a shape, strides and an offset, so that slicing, transposing and reshaping make views that share memory while fancy (index-list) selection copies; zero-based indexing, negative indices, half-open slices, boolean masks; the dtype (fixed-width integers wrap around on overflow, `float64` has machine epsilon 2.2·10⁻¹⁶, `float32` 1.2·10⁻⁷); universal functions and reductions along an axis; broadcasting (align the shapes from the right, a length-1 axis is stretched by giving it stride 0, any other mismatch is an error) and how it differs from the silent recycling of R; the cost model of vectorisation (one Python-level call over a million elements against a million interpreted steps). Missing data: `NaN` in floating arrays (it propagates, `nan == nan` is false, `nanmean` skips it), the pandas missing value and nullable dtypes, the `skipna` rule. The data frame: `Series` and `DataFrame`, the index and automatic alignment, `loc` and `iloc`, boolean selection, `groupby` as split–apply–combine, `merge` as a join (inner, left, outer; duplicate keys multiply rows), reading a CSV file, `describe`. Distributions in SciPy: the methods `pmf` or `pdf`, `cdf`, `sf`, `ppf` and `rvs` of a distribution object, frozen distributions, the parameter conventions (`scale` is a standard deviation for the normal and the reciprocal of the rate for the exponential). Random numbers: `numpy.random.default_rng(seed)`, the PCG64 generator, why a seed gives the same stream within one library version but not across languages, spawning independent streams, the Box–Muller transform. The formula interface: `y ~ x1 + x2 + x1:x2 + C(g)` as a small language, how patsy turns it into a design matrix (the intercept column, treatment coding of a categorical variable with one level dropped, the interaction as a product, the order in which columns are placed), `statsmodels.formula.api.ols` and `glm`, reading a regression summary. Plotting: Matplotlib figure and axes, histogram, scatter, line, error bars, saving to a file, and why a histogram is a count per bin. Environment: `pip`, virtual environments, imports, running a script and a notebook. The R-to-Python crosswalk used wherever the course speaks of R: vector (ndarray), `1:n` (`np.arange(1, n + 1)`, since indices start at 0), recycling (broadcasting, stricter), `NA` (`np.nan` or the pandas missing value), `data.frame` (`DataFrame`), the `apply` family (comprehensions, vectorised calls, `groupby`), `dnorm`, `pnorm`, `qnorm` and `rnorm` (`pdf`, `cdf`, `ppf`, `rvs`), `set.seed` (`default_rng(seed)`), `lm` and `glm` (`ols` and `glm` of statsmodels), `ggplot2` and base graphics (Matplotlib, seaborn), `install.packages` and `library` (`pip install` and `import`), `brms` (Bambi) and Stan (PyMC, with CmdStanPy as the route to Stan itself).

### T0803

Used by: 6fz

- **Results:** Count-Min with width ⌈e/ε⌉ and depth ⌈ln(1/δ)⌉ never underestimates and overestimates by more than εN with probability at most δ [P, Markov and independence across rows; check: with ε = 0.001 and δ = 0.01 the table has 2719×5 = 13,595 cells for 13,638 distinct items, the largest overcount is 30 against εN = 197, and no estimate is below the truth]; the Count sketch estimate is unbiased with error about ‖f‖₂/√w [P; check: 5 rows of 2000 counters on the same stream give a maximum error of 224 against ‖f‖₂/√w = 1305]; for a random permutation P[min h(A) = min h(B)] = J(A, B) [P], so with 128 hashes the estimate has standard deviation √(J(1 − J)/128) = 0.044, observed 0.045 [check]; a linear hash family (ax + b) mod p is not min-wise independent: on two ranges of consecutive integers with J = 0.5 it estimates 0.435, while random permutations give 0.499, and on random sets the linear family is unbiased (0.504) [check]; with b = 20 bands of r = 5 rows the candidate probability 1 − (1 − s⁵)²⁰ is 0.047 at s = 0.3, 0.47 at 0.5, 0.64 at 0.55 and 0.9996 at 0.8, with the threshold near (1/b)^(1/r) = 0.549 [D, check]; for random hyperplanes P[sign(r·u) = sign(r·v)] = 1 − θ/π [P, check: 0.7745 against 0.7759]; an exact kd-tree nearest-neighbour search on 5000 uniform points computes about 5 distances in 2 dimensions, 424 in 8, 4797 in 16 and all 5000 in 32, which is the curse of dimensionality [check].

In this unit: chain of responsibility (apply a chain of successive handlers to try to process the data), command (bundle a command and its arguments to call later), interpreter (define a grammar for a language and use it to interpret statements), iterator (traverse a container and access its elements, in two implementations, the second marked alt. impl. in the source), mediator (an object that knows how to connect other objects and acts as a proxy), memento (generate an opaque token that can go back to a previous state).

- **Topics:** The System Design Primer (Donne Martin) and its Motivation: learn how to design large-scale systems, learn from the open source community, and prep for the system design interview; the Index of system design topics, where everything is a trade-off; the Anki flashcards (spaced-repetition decks) and the sister Coding resource, the interactive coding challenges. The Study guide: suggested topics to review depending on your interview timeline (short, medium or long: breadth first, then depth), with the answer that you do not need to know everything, and that you should start broad and go deeper in a few areas. How to approach a system design interview question: the interview is an open-ended conversation that you lead; Step 1 outline use cases, constraints and assumptions (who will use it and how, how many users, what the system does, its inputs and outputs, how much data, how many requests per second, the read-to-write ratio); Step 2 create a high-level design (sketch the main components and connections, justify them); Step 3 design core components (for a url shortener: the hash of the full url with MD5 and Base62, hash collisions, SQL or NoSQL, the database schema, translating a hash back to the url, the API and object-oriented design); Step 4 scale the design (identify bottlenecks and address them with a load balancer, horizontal scaling, caching, database sharding, stating the trade-offs). System design topics: start here, for a newcomer: Step 1 review the scalability video lecture (vertical and horizontal scaling, caching, load balancing, database replication and partitioning), Step 2 review the scalability article (clones, databases, caches, asynchronism), then the next steps, the three high-level trade-offs (performance versus scalability, latency versus throughput, availability versus consistency), then DNS, CDNs and load balancers. The Appendix: back-of-the-envelope estimates, the powers of two table (power, exact value, approximate value, bytes), and the latency numbers every programmer should know (L1 cache reference 0.5 ns, branch mispredict 5 ns, L2 cache reference 7 ns, mutex lock/unlock 25 ns, main memory reference 100 ns, compress 1K bytes 10 µs, send 1 KB over a 1 Gbps network 10 µs, read 4 KB randomly from SSD 150 µs, read 1 MB sequentially from memory 250 µs, round trip within same datacenter 500 µs, read 1 MB sequentially from SSD 1 ms, HDD seek 10 ms, read 1 MB sequentially from 1 Gbps Ethernet 10 ms, read 1 MB sequentially from HDD 30 ms, send packet CA->Netherlands->CA 150 ms), the latency numbers visualized, and the handy metrics derived from them.

### T0873

Used by: ee, 2a8, 6w3, 7yu, 88u, 95n, blf, bma, bmb, bmc, bmd, bmi, bmr, dck, dld, du1, ee5, fan, gbp, gce, gom, h9m, iye, j9l, jbl, jg5, jmn, l2n, l2p, l6h, l6l, laf, lcq, lcv, lx8, mdj, mdw, mwe, n3v, n9i, ngd, nnl, nrm, oda, pd4, psp, qkx, qm3, qxy, qz6, rab, rg1

- **Topics:** performance versus scalability (a service is scalable if added resources raise performance in proportion; a performance problem means your system is slow for a single user; a scalability problem means it is fast for a single user but slow under heavy load); latency versus throughput (latency is the time to perform an action, throughput the number of actions per unit of time; aim for maximal throughput with acceptable latency). The domain name system: the hierarchy with a few authoritative servers at the top, caching and propagation delays, the NS record (name server), MX record (mail exchange), A record (address) and CNAME (canonical), managed DNS services (CloudFlare, Route 53) that route traffic to avoid servers under maintenance, balance between varying cluster sizes and run A/B tests, and the disadvantages (an added delay, management complexity, DDoS exposure); the protocol itself is in U2.4. The content delivery network: a globally distributed network of proxy servers serving from locations near the user, push CDNs (you upload content when it changes, suited to low traffic or rarely changing content), pull CDNs (the CDN fetches on the first request and caches for a time-to-live, suited to heavy traffic), and the disadvantages (cost, stale content before the TTL expires, changed urls); the caching theory is in U3.11. The load balancer: distributing requests to application servers and databases, preventing requests to unhealthy servers, preventing overload, removing a single point of failure; hardware or software (HAProxy); SSL termination; session persistence; routing metrics (random choice, least loaded, session or cookies), layer 4 (transport headers only) or layer 7 (application content: it terminates the connection, reads the message, chooses a backend and opens a new connection); active-passive or active-active pairs; horizontal scaling (scale out on commodity machines, versus vertical scaling on one bigger machine), why servers should be stateless and keep sessions in a centralised store (a database or a persistent cache such as Redis or Memcached), and the disadvantages of a load balancer and of horizontal scaling. The reverse proxy (web server): one front for internal services with increased security, scalability and flexibility, SSL termination, compression, caching and static content, how it differs from a load balancer (a load balancer helps when there are several servers of one function; a reverse proxy helps even with one), NGINX and HAProxy, and its disadvantages. The application layer: separating the web layer from the application (platform) layer so each scales and is configured independently, the single responsibility principle, workers that enable asynchronism, microservices as independently deployable small modular services with a lightweight interface (the Pinterest example: user profile, follower, feed, search, photo upload), service discovery (Consul, Etcd, ZooKeeper with health checks done using an HTTP endpoint and a built-in key-value store; the recipes are in U9.15), and the operational cost of loose coupling.

### T0874

Used by: 4jz, 4pf, 5fm, 5ld, bl8, bl9, bli, blj, bm4, bm5, bmj, drg, ej1, ezf, g74, jk3, l9z, lg6, mkx, n91, n92, njf, nji, nk9, nka, p3u, p47, pl4, ppt, pqm, r2e, r2g, r78, rki

- **Topics:** availability versus consistency and the CAP theorem (consistency: every read receives the most recent write or an error; availability: every request receives a response, not necessarily the latest; partition tolerance: the system continues despite network partitions): since networks are not reliable you must support partition tolerance and choose between consistency and availability, with CP (consistency and partition tolerance: waiting for the partitioned node may time out, a good choice if the business needs atomic reads and writes) and AP (availability and partition tolerance: return the most readily available, perhaps stale, version; writes propagate after the partition heals; a good choice for eventual consistency or when the system must keep working despite external errors); the theory and the proof are in U9.16. Consistency patterns: weak consistency (after a write, reads may or may not see it, best effort; memcached, and real-time uses such as VoIP, video chat and multiplayer games), eventual consistency (reads eventually see the write, typically within milliseconds, data replicated asynchronously; DNS and email) and strong consistency (reads see the write, data replicated synchronously; file systems and RDBMSes, suited to transactions). Availability patterns: fail-over (active-passive: heartbeats between the active and the passive standby, and if they stop the passive takes over the active's IP address, with downtime set by hot standby versus cold standby and only the active serving traffic; active-active: both serve and share load, so public servers need both addresses in DNS and internal ones need application logic that knows both; the disadvantages of failover are extra hardware, complexity and potential data loss if the active fails before replication) and replication (master-slave and master-master, in U16.11); availability in numbers: the percentage of uptime, counted in nines, with the tables for 99.9% (three 9s) and 99.99% (four 9s) per year, month, week and day, and availability in parallel versus in sequence.

### T0875

Used by: l2c

- **Results:** 99.9% allows 8 h 45 min 57.6 s of downtime a year (the primer truncates to 57 s), 43 min 49.8 s a month, 10 min 4.8 s a week and 86.4 s a day, and 99.99% allows 52.60 min a year, 263 s a month, **60.5 s a week** and 8.64 s a day; the primer's table gives "1m 5s" a week for four nines, which is wrong by the recomputation (recorded in Appendix E) [D, check]; components in sequence multiply availability (two at 99.9% give 0.998001) and components in parallel multiply unavailability (two at 99.9% give 1 − 0.001² = 0.999999), so five components in sequence at 99.9% give 99.50% and three in parallel give 99.9999999% [D, check]; every extra 9 divides the yearly downtime budget by 10, but the budget is also spent by detection and switch-over: a heartbeat every second with 3 missed beats plus a 5 s hot switch is 8 s per fail-over, four a year is 32 s, while a 5-minute cold start four times a year is 20 minutes, which is two-fifths of the four-nines budget [D, check]; with asynchronous replication a read from a lagging replica returns stale data if a write arrived in the last L seconds, so for writes at 0.5 per second and a lag of 0.2 s the stale fraction is 1 − e^(−0.5 × 0.2) = 9.5%, and a simulation gave 9.6% [D, check]; CAP's choice is per operation, not per system: a shopping cart can be AP while the payment is CP [S].

### T0877

Used by: 2v7, 3ju, 70g, blk, blm, blo, blp, blq, bm2, bm6, bmf, bmk, byv, c1y, c5a, cd7, dbk, dft, e36, esf, h9e, ifg, k47, kz1, l2t, l48, l49, lf6, ljw, lp6, lsr, ly5, m00, m45, mdn, mgm, mj6, mu9, mup, nib, njs, ns6, o9f, ob9, oq7, oxl, p4d, pel, ps4, pv5, q3t, qfp, qzw

- **Topics:** the relational database management system (RDBMS) as a collection of tables with the ACID properties (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability; the theory is in U15.20) and the six techniques the primer lists to scale it: master-slave replication (the master serves reads and writes and replicates to slaves that serve reads, in a tree if needed; if the master fails the system runs read-only until a slave is promoted); master-master replication (both serve reads and writes and coordinate on writes; a load balancer or application logic decides where to write; loose consistency or higher write latency; conflict resolution) and the disadvantages of replication (possible data loss, replicas bogged down replaying writes, replication lag growing with more slaves, single-threaded replay, extra hardware); federation or functional partitioning (separate forums, users and products databases, less traffic and lag each, but joins across databases are harder and the application must know where to go); sharding (distribute data across databases so each holds a subset, such as users by last-name initial or by geography; less traffic, replication and index size and more cache hits; the disadvantages are application complexity, lopsided data from power users, rebalancing, hard joins; consistent hashing reduces the data moved); denormalization (redundant copies to avoid expensive joins, for example materialized views, since reads can outnumber writes 100:1 or 1000:1; the disadvantages are duplicated data and heavy-write cost); SQL tuning (benchmark with a load tool and profile with the slow query log; tighten the schema: CHAR for fixed length, TEXT for large text, INT up to 2^32, DECIMAL for currency, no large BLOBs, VARCHAR(255) and the 8-bit length, NOT NULL; use good indices (B-trees, extra space and slower writes, disabling indices during a bulk load); avoid expensive joins; partition tables; tune the query cache). NoSQL as key-value store (abstraction: hash table), document store (key-value store with documents as values, for example MongoDB, CouchDB and DynamoDB), wide column store (nested map of column families, row key and timestamp; Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra) and graph database (abstraction: graph); BASE (basically available, soft state, eventual consistency); SQL or NoSQL: the primer's reasons for SQL (structured data, strict schema, relational data, complex joins, transactions, clear patterns for scaling, established tools, fast index lookups) and for NoSQL (semi-structured data, dynamic or flexible schema, non-relational data, no complex joins, many TB or PB of data, data-intensive workload, very high IOPS throughput) and the sample data well-suited for NoSQL (clickstream and log ingest, leaderboard or scoring data, temporary data such as a shopping cart, hot tables, metadata and lookup tables).

### T0879

Used by: 4bx, 5ek, blt, blu, blv, blw, blx, bly, bme, bms, crm, glv, l33, l37, lbb, lf7, ltk, luq, lvu, mt3, n6u, n6v, nde, o9s, ogo, oky, opl, p0u, pnd, q33, r74

- **Topics:** why cache (shorter page loads, less load on servers and databases, absorbing uneven loads and spikes); where: client caching (the OS or browser), CDN caching, web server caching (reverse proxies and caches such as Varnish), database caching (default settings tuned to a generic load), application caching (in-memory key-value stores such as Memcached and Redis between the application and storage; Redis adds persistence and built-in data structures such as sorted sets and lists; avoid file-based caching because it hampers cloning and autoscaling); what: caching at the database query level (hash the query as the key; expiry is hard because one changed cell invalidates every cached query that might include it) and caching at the object level (assemble the data into a class instance, remove it when the underlying data changes, which also lets workers consume the latest cached object; suggested contents: user sessions, fully rendered web pages, activity streams, user graph data); when to update the cache: cache-aside (the application reads and writes storage and the cache stays passive: on a miss load from the database, add to the cache and return; lazy loading; each miss costs three trips and entries can go stale, limited by a TTL or write-through; a failed node is replaced by an empty one), write-through (the application writes to the cache as the main store and the cache writes synchronously to the data store; reads of just-written data are fast and data is not stale, but writes are slow and most written data might never be read), write-behind or write-back (add or update the cache and write to the store asynchronously; better write performance, risk of data loss if the cache fails first, more complex) and refresh-ahead (refresh recently accessed entries before they expire; lower latency if the access prediction is right, worse if it is wrong); the disadvantages of caches: keeping them consistent with the source of truth by cache invalidation, which is a hard problem, and changing the application.

- **Topics:** asynchronism (expensive operations out of the request path, and work done in advance such as periodic aggregation): message queues (an application publishes a job and tells the user its status, a worker takes it, processes it and signals completion, while the client may show a small amount of optimistic work; Redis as a simple message broker whose messages can be lost, RabbitMQ with its AMQP protocol and self-managed nodes, Amazon SQS hosted but with higher latency and possible double delivery), task queues (receive tasks with data, run them and deliver results, with scheduling; Celery, mainly for Python), back pressure (a queue that outgrows memory means cache misses and disk reads, so limit the queue size and answer busy), and the disadvantage that cheap or real-time work is better synchronous. Communication: the hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP) as a request and response protocol with a verb and a resource, and the verbs GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE with their idempotent, safe and cacheable columns; the transmission control protocol (TCP: connection-oriented, handshake, sequence numbers and checksums, retransmission, flow control, congestion control, many open connections costing memory, connection pooling; use it when all data must arrive intact); the user datagram protocol (UDP: connectionless datagrams that may arrive out of order or not at all, broadcast as with DHCP, no congestion control; use it for lowest latency, when late data is worse than lost data, or for your own error correction, as in VoIP, video chat, streaming and games); the remote procedure call (the call chain client program, client stub marshalling the procedure id and arguments, client and server communication modules, server stub unmarshalling and calling the server procedure, the reply in reverse; focused on exposing behaviours, tightly coupled, hard to debug and cache); representational state transfer (a client and server architecture on resources with stateless communication; four qualities: identify resources by a URI, change them through representations (verbs, headers and body), self-descriptive errors (status codes), and HATEOAS; focused on exposing data, usual for public APIs; its disadvantages: awkward when resources are not a simple hierarchy, few verbs, several round trips for nested data, payload bloat as fields grow); the table comparing RPC and REST calls (signup, resign, read a person, read a person's items, add an item, update an item, delete an item); security basics: encrypt in transit and at rest, sanitize all user inputs to prevent XSS and SQL injection, use parameterized queries, apply the principle of least privilege (the depth is in U5.18, U6.7 and U7.7).

### T0884

Used by: 2ha, 41p, 42h, 4hq, 789, 7fn, bez, bkw, bkx, bvy, el5, elb, ffv, ghg, gkt, jb9, jzy, ke2, l7j, l7k, lb6, lbr, lbv, le7, lem, len, lgm, lgn, lgo, lgr, lo6, lpu, ls3, lty, lue, m6f, mb1, ml0, mm5, mtl, nb3, ncx, niz, o5o, o8i, o8k, o8l, odb, oxz, p4o, p4q, pe9, pv7, q17, q18, q1y, q4f, qdx, qo3, qor, qq3, qw4, qw8, qxa

- **Topics:** the Primer's system design interview questions with solutions (Pastebin.com or Bit.ly, the Twitter timeline and search or Facebook feed and search, a web crawler, Mint.com, the data structures for a social network, a key-value store for a search engine, Amazon's sales ranking by category, scaling to millions of users on AWS), each worked in the same four steps: Step 1 outline use cases and constraints (use cases, out of scope, constraints and assumptions, state assumptions, calculate usage), Step 2 create a high level design, Step 3 design core components (one use case at a time), Step 4 scale the design, and then additional talking points (SQL scaling patterns, NoSQL, caching, asynchronism and microservices, communications, security, latency numbers). Design Pastebin.com (or Bit.ly): use cases: the user enters a block of text and gets a randomly generated link (with an optional expiration), the user enters a paste's url and views the contents, the service tracks analytics of pages (monthly visit statistics), the service deletes expired pastes, high availability; out of scope: accounts, email verification, editing, visibility, custom shortlinks; assumptions: traffic is not evenly distributed, following a short link should be fast, pastes are text only, analytics need not be realtime, 10 million users, 10 million paste writes and 100 million reads a month (10:1); usage: about 1.27 KB per paste (1 KB content, a 7-byte shortlink, a 4-byte expiration length, a 5-byte created-at, a 255-byte path), 12.7 GB a month, about 450 GB and 360 million shortlinks in 3 years, 4 writes and 40 reads per second. Core: a relational database as a large hash table from the url to a path on a file server, or an object store such as S3 or a NoSQL document or key-value store; the web server as a reverse proxy to a Write API and a Read API; the `pastes` table keyed on `shortlink`; the url from the MD5 hash of the user's IP address plus a timestamp, Base62-encoded (digits and letters, unlike Base64's `+` and `/`) and cut to the first 7 characters; a public REST API and RPC inside; analytics by MapReduce over the web server logs, and expiry by scanning for pastes older than the current timestamp; scaling: an analytics database (a data warehouse such as Redshift or BigQuery), an object store, a memory cache for the 40 reads a second, SQL write master-slave and the other SQL scaling patterns. Design the Twitter timeline and search (or Facebook feed and search): use cases: a user posts a tweet, views the home timeline (people followed), views the user timeline, searches keywords, with notifications and fan-out in scope; assumptions: 100 million active users, 500 million tweets a day (15 billion a month) with an average fan-out of 10 (5 billion deliveries a day), 250 billion reads and 10 billion searches a month, reads far outnumber writes; usage: about 10 KB per tweet (8-byte id, 32-byte user id, 140 bytes of text, about 10 KB of media), 150 TB a month and 5.4 PB in 3 years, 100 thousand reads, 6,000 tweets, 60 thousand fan-out deliveries and 4,000 searches a second. Core: the Write API stores the tweet in the user timeline (SQL) and calls the Fan Out Service, which asks the User Graph Service for followers (kept in the memory cache), pushes the tweet into each follower's home timeline in a Memory Cache (a Redis list of tweet id, user id and metadata, 17 bytes per entry), indexes it in the Search Index Service, stores media in the Object Store and sends push notifications through the Notification Service; the Read API asks the Timeline Service for the cached ids (O(1)) and does multiget calls to the Tweet Info and User Info Services (O(n)); search tokenises the query and asks a Search Cluster such as Lucene; scaling: the fan-out service is the bottleneck for users with millions of followers (so skip fan-out for them and merge their tweets in at read time), keep only a few hundred tweets per cached timeline and only active users' timelines (rebuild from SQL if inactive for 30 days), keep a month of tweets, keep the search index in memory, and add SQL scaling patterns.

- **Topics:** Design a web crawler: use cases (the service crawls a list of urls, a user inputs a search term and sees pages with titles and snippets), assumptions (anonymous users, no infinite loop on a cyclic graph, 1 billion links to crawl and refreshed about weekly so 4 billion crawled a month, 500 KB per page, 100 billion searches a month, and no existing system such as Solr or Nutch), usage (2 PB a month, 72 PB in 3 years, 1,600 writes and 40,000 searches a second); core: ranked `links_to_crawl` (Redis sorted sets) and `crawled_links` with page signatures in a NoSQL store, a Crawler Service loop taking the top ranked link, classes PagesDataStore, Page and Crawler; handling duplicates (sort and unique for small lists, MapReduce keeping entries with frequency 1 for a billion links, and a content signature compared with the Jaccard index or cosine similarity); determining when to update the crawl results (a timestamp and a default one-week refresh, mean time between page changes, robots.txt); the search path (Query API, Reverse Index Service, Document Service); scaling (cache popular queries, shard and federate the index and document stores, the crawler's own DNS cache, connection pooling). Design Mint.com: use cases (the user connects to a financial account, the service extracts transactions from the account, the service recommends a budget, then the user accesses summaries and transactions), assumptions (10 million users with 10 budget categories each, 50,000 sellers, 30 million financial accounts, 5 billion transactions and 500 million reads a month, write-heavy 10:1, daily refresh for users active in the last 30 days), usage (about 50 bytes per transaction, 250 GB a month, 9 TB in 3 years, 2,000 writes and 200 reads a second); core: an Accounts API writing the `accounts` table, extraction through a queue (SQS or RabbitMQ) with a Transaction Extraction Service that stores raw logs in the object store, categorises through the Category Service (a seller-to-category dictionary, 50,000 sellers at under 255 bytes each, about 12 MB, with a heap of the top manual override per seller), and updates the `transactions` and `monthly_spending` tables; the Budget Service with a generic template by income tier (housing 40%, food 20%, gas 10%, shopping 20%) so only overrides are stored, aggregation in SQL or by MapReduce on the raw files; scaling (memory cache for sessions, aggregates and recent transactions, an analytics database such as Redshift or BigQuery, a month of transactions in the database and the rest in the object store). Design the data structures for a social network: use cases (a user searches for someone and sees the shortest path to the searched person), assumptions (graph data does not fit one machine, unweighted edges, 100 million users, 50 friends each so 5 billion friend relationships, 1 billion searches a month so 400 a second, no graph database or GraphQL), core: breadth-first search, with users sharded across Person Servers behind a Lookup Service and a User Graph Service running the search (classes Person, PersonServer, LookupService); further optimisations (cache complete or partial BFS traversals, batch offline into NoSQL, batch friend lookups on the same Person Server and shard by location, run two BFS searches from source and destination and merge, start from high-degree people, set a limit on time or hops before asking the user, or use a graph database such as Neo4j if allowed). Design a key-value store for a search engine: use case (a request that hits the cache), assumptions (popular queries nearly always cached, limited memory, millions of queries, 10 million users, 10 billion queries a month), usage (270 bytes per entry: 50-byte query, 20-byte title, 200-byte snippet; 2.7 TB a month if all unique; 4,000 requests a second); core: a memory cache with LRU expiry from a doubly linked list plus a hash table (classes Node, LinkedList, Cache), updated by TTL (cache-aside); scaling by expanding the memory cache to many machines in three ways (each machine its own cache, each with a copy, or the cache sharded by hashing the query). Design Amazon's sales ranking by category: use cases (the service calculates the past week's most popular products by category, a user views them), assumptions (10 million products, 1,000 categories, 1 billion transactions and 100 billion reads a month, 100:1, results updated hourly, items in several categories but never changing category), usage (about 40 bytes per transaction, 40 GB a month, 1.44 TB in 3 years, 400 writes and 40,000 reads a second), core: sales logs in the object store, a multi-step MapReduce (step 1 transform to `(category, product_id), sum(quantity)`, step 2 a distributed sort) writing a `sales_rank` table, read through the cache. Each of the five follows the template of U16.14: Outline use cases and constraints (use cases, out of scope, constraints and assumptions, state assumptions), Create a high level design, Design core components, Scale the design, and Additional talking points (SQL scaling patterns, NoSQL, caching, asynchronism, communications, security); the key-value cache design adds a Cache implementation section (the linked list, hash table and TTL update above).

- **Topics:** Design a system that scales to millions of users on AWS: use case: a user makes a read or write request; assumptions (relational data needed, 10 million users, 1 billion writes and 100 billion reads a month, 100:1, 1 KB per write), usage (1 TB a month, 36 TB in 3 years, 400 writes and 40,000 reads a second); Goals for 1-2 users: a single box, vertical scaling, and monitoring (CPU, memory, I/O, network; CloudWatch, top, Nagios, statsd, Graphite); start with a single box (web server and a MySQL database on one EC2 instance; vertical scaling gets expensive and has no redundancy); start with SQL, consider NoSQL; assign a public static IP (an elastic IP helps fail-over, since you point the domain at a new address); use a DNS (Route 53); secure the web server (open ports 80, 443 and 22 only from whitelisted IPs, no outbound connections). Scale the design in stages: Users+: assumptions (the single box is loaded, benchmarks and profiling point at MySQL), store static content separately in an object store (S3) and move the MySQL database to a separate box (RDS), secure the system (encrypt in transit and at rest, a virtual private cloud with a public subnet for the web server and a private one for the rest); Users++: horizontal scaling behind a load balancer (ELB or HAProxy, SSL terminated there), several web servers across availability zones, master-slave MySQL fail-over, separate web servers from application servers (a reverse proxy; read and write APIs), a CDN (CloudFront); Users+++ (read-heavy 100:1): a memory cache (Elasticache) for hot MySQL content and session data (so the web servers are stateless), add MySQL read replicas with a load balancer in front, and more servers; Users++++: add autoscaling (an autoscaling group per server type across zones, min and max sizes, triggers from CloudWatch on time of day, CPU load, latency, network traffic or a custom metric; the disadvantages are complexity and lag) and automate DevOps (Chef, Puppet, Ansible), with monitoring at host, aggregate, log, external-site, notification and error-reporting levels; Users+++++: keep iterating on benchmarks, a data warehouse (Redshift) for older data, and SQL scaling patterns and NoSQL. Additional system design interview questions, as the Primer lists them with reading: a file sync service like Dropbox, a search engine like Google, a scalable web crawler like Google, Google docs, a key-value store like Redis, a cache system like Memcached, a recommendation system like Amazon's, a tinyurl system like Bitly, a chat app like WhatsApp, a picture sharing system like Instagram, the Facebook news feed, the Facebook timeline, the Facebook chat function, a graph search function like Facebook's, a content delivery network like CloudFlare, a trending topic system like Twitter's, a random ID generation system, returning the top k requests during a time interval, a system that serves data from multiple data centers, an online multiplayer card game, a garbage collection system, an API rate limiter, and a stock exchange (like NASDAQ or Binance). Real-world architectures, by type: data processing (MapReduce, Spark, Storm), data store (Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB, Spanner, Memcached, Redis), file system (the Google File System, HDFS) and miscellaneous (Chubby, Dapper, Kafka, ZooKeeper); company architectures (Amazon, Cinchcast, DataSift, Dropbox, ESPN, Google, Instagram, Justin.tv, Facebook, Flickr, Mailbox, Netflix, Pinterest, Playfish, PlentyOfFish, Salesforce, Stack Overflow, TripAdvisor, Tumblr, Twitter, Uber, WhatsApp, YouTube); and the company engineering blogs the Primer lists (for the companies you will meet). ### T0891

Used by: 49s, 4z3, 71l, 7g0, 8z7, 99f, aj8, anq, asr, auz, avk, avr, bf9, bvd, bvh, f99, fbk, g4k, jca, lkg, mc3, mcx, mlt, mxi, n04, n0v, n12, nqy, opv, qui, r6w

- **Topics:** Introduction to Computing (the introductory course's Week 1): what a computer is (a machine that executes a stored program of instructions over data held in memory), the von Neumann organisation (processor, memory, input and output, with program and data in one memory), the layers from transistors and gates through the instruction set to the operating system and programs, and why everything is reduced to binary. Evolution of Computer Systems (the organisation course's Week 1): from mechanical calculators and the stored-program idea through vacuum tubes, transistors and integrated circuits to microprocessors and multicore chips; Moore's law as an observation about transistor counts and the end of Dennard scaling as the reason clock rates stopped rising and cores multiplied (history recalled, not checked). Number Systems (Week 2): binary representations and positional number systems in base 2, 8, 10 and 16, conversion between bases by repeated division and by grouping bits; unsigned integers and their range; signed representations: sign-magnitude, 1's complement (one's complement, with its two zeros) and 2's complement (two's complement); negation, sign extension, addition and subtraction of signed numbers and the overflow rule; bit-level operations (AND, OR, XOR, shifts, masks). Boolean algebra and gate-level logic: the axioms, De Morgan's laws, truth tables, sum-of-products and product-of-sums forms, Karnaugh-map minimisation, NAND and NOR as universal gates. Combinational building blocks: decoder, encoder, multiplexer, comparator, half and full adder, ripple-carry adder, a small ALU. Sequential logic: SR and D latches, edge-triggered D flip-flops, registers and counters, finite-state machines in Moore and Mealy form. Clocked timing: clock-to-Q delay, setup and hold times, the critical path and the maximum clock frequency, clock skew.

- **Topics:** Basic Computer Organization (the multicore course's Week 1): Review of Basic Computer Organization, Basic operational concepts (fetch, decode, execute, the program counter, the instruction and memory address registers), the fundamental of program execution (the instruction cycle and how a high-level statement becomes a sequence of instructions), memory and I/O addressing (byte addressing, alignment, little- and big-endian order; memory-mapped versus isolated I/O). Instruction Set Architecture (the organisation course's Week 2, and MCA Week 1): the instruction set as the contract between hardware and software; operand storage classes (stack, accumulator, register-memory, load-store); addressing modes (immediate, register, register indirect, base plus displacement, indexed, PC-relative, auto-increment as pre- and post-index); the instruction set itself (data transfer, arithmetic and logic, control flow, system); instruction encoding and formats (fixed versus variable length, field layout, expanding opcodes, immediates and their sign extension); CISC vs RISC ISA (the RISC principles: load-store, fixed-length encoding, many registers, simple addressing; the CISC trade-off of code density against decode complexity; modern x86 decoding into micro-operations, recalled, not checked). Assembly Language I and II (the introductory course's Weeks 4 and 5): registers and the zero register, arithmetic, logic and shift instructions, loads and stores, compare and conditional branches, loops and if-then-else, arrays and pointers, functions and procedure calls (branch-and-link, the return address, the stack and stack frames, caller- and callee-saved registers, the calling convention), recursion. Review of Traditional Computer Architecture (the GPU course's Week 1): the Basic five stage RISC Pipeline, Cache Memory, the Register File, and SIMD instructions, reviewed here from the instruction-set side and treated in depth in U14.6, U14.9 and U14.8. ### T0895

Used by: cxq, l2v

- **Crosswalk (A64 ↔ MIPS-like ↔ RISC-V-like; recalled, not checked, and the encodings below are recomputed by script):**

| Concept | A64 | MIPS-like | RISC-V-like |
|---|---|---|---|
| General registers | X0–X30 (64-bit), W0–W30 (low 32 bits); encoding 31 is XZR or SP by context | $0–$31, $zero hard-wired | x0–x31, x0 hard-wired zero |
| Register add | `ADD X0, X1, X2` = 0x8B020020 | `add $t0, $s1, $s2` = 0x02324020 | `add x10, x1, x2` = 0x00208533 |
| Immediate add | `ADD X0, X1, #imm12` (optionally shifted by 12) | `addi $t0, $s1, imm16` | `addi x10, x1, imm12` |
| Load and store | `LDR X0, [X1, #8]`; pre-index `[X1, #8]!`; post-index `[X1], #8`; pairs `LDP`/`STP` | `lw $t0, 8($s1)` | `ld x10, 8(x1)` |
| Compare and branch | `CMP X1, X2` sets NZCV, then `B.LT label` (19-bit word offset, ±1 MiB) | `slt` then `bne`/`beq` (16-bit word offset, ±128 KiB), with a delay slot | `blt x1, x2, label` (no flags) |
| Branch on zero | `CBZ X0, label` / `CBNZ` | `beq $t0, $zero, label` | `beqz x10, label` |
| Call and return | `BL f` puts the return address in X30; `RET` | `jal f` ($ra); `jr $ra` | `jal ra, f`; `ret` |
| Unconditional branch | `B label` (26-bit word offset, ±128 MiB) | `j target` (26-bit pseudo-direct) | `jal x0, label` |

### T0896

Used by: mpg

- **Results:** The four classes of operand storage and the RISC argument from instruction frequencies [S, from the measured dominance of simple instructions]; a branch field of k bits holding a signed word offset reaches ±2^{k−1}·4 bytes, so A64 `B` reaches ±128 MiB, `B.cond` and `CBZ` reach ±1 MiB with largest forward offset 1 048 572 bytes, and a MIPS `beq` reaches ±128 KiB [D]; the encodings in the crosswalk follow from the field layouts (MIPS R-type opcode 0, rs 17, rt 18, rd 8, funct 0x20 gives 0x02324020) [check]; an expanding opcode trades the number of operand fields against opcode space: in a 16-bit instruction of four 4-bit fields, using 15 primary opcode patterns for three-address instructions leaves one escape pattern for 16 two-address ones [D]; little-endian and big-endian orders agree on single bytes and differ by byte reversal on words [Def]; the procedure-call stack discipline (push the frame on entry, pop on exit) makes recursion work because each activation has its own frame [S]; memory-mapped I/O needs no extra instructions but uses address space, isolated I/O needs IN and OUT instructions [Def].

### T0899

Used by: 1ae

- **Results:** The iron law: time = instruction count × CPI × clock period [D]; CPI of a mix is Σ f_i·CPI_i, so the mix 45% ALU at 1, 25% loads at 4, 10% stores at 3 and 20% branches at 2 gives CPI 2.15 and 1488 MIPS at 3.2 GHz [D, check]; MIPS ranks machines wrongly when instruction counts differ [S, by a counterexample]; for equal work, the right mean of rates is the harmonic mean (1000 and 250 MIPS on equal work give 400, the total work over the total time) and the right mean of times is the arithmetic mean [P]; AM ≥ GM ≥ HM [P]; the geometric mean of normalised ratios is independent of the reference machine, since GM(a_i/r_i)/GM(b_i/r_i) = GM(a_i/b_i) [P]; Amdahl's law (proved in U11.1) applied: enhancing 40% of the time by a factor 10 gives 1.5625 overall [check]; availability = MTTF/(MTTF + MTTR) [Def]; dies per wafer ≈ π(d/2)²/A − πd/√(2A), giving about 416.8 for a 30 cm wafer and 1.5 cm² dies [check, formula recalled, not checked against a source].

- **Topics:** Theory of memory models (the advanced course's Week 9): a memory model as the set of values a load may return; program order, the global memory order and the "reads from" relation; sequential consistency as some total order consistent with every program order; total store order (TSO, the x86 model) with store buffers and forwarding; relaxed models (release consistency, the ARM and RISC-V weak models) that let independent accesses be reordered unless ordered by fences, acquire and release, or dependencies; litmus tests (store buffering SB, message passing MP, load buffering LB, independent reads of independent writes IRIW) and axiomatic versus operational definitions. Memory consistency models- Sequential, Relaxed consistency models (the parallel architecture course's Week 10): Lamport's definition, the conditions program order and write atomicity, how write buffers, non-blocking caches and out-of-order execution break sequential consistency, and the processor-consistency, weak-ordering and release-consistency families. Synchronization- LL-SC, point to point, barrier synchronization (Week 11): atomic read-modify-write instructions (test-and-set, swap, fetch-and-add, compare-and-swap), load-linked and store-conditional, test-and-test-and-set, ticket and queue-based (MCS) locks, point-to-point synchronisation with flags, centralised sense-reversing, tree and dissemination barriers. Cache coherence and memory consistency (the multicore course's Week 8): the consistency half here, the coherence half in U14.14.

### T0926

Used by: nc4, o1a, s37

- **Results:** A litmus-test enumerator finds that SB has three outcomes under sequential consistency, with r1 = r2 = 0 forbidden, while an operational TSO model with FIFO store buffers and forwarding allows r1 = r2 = 0 [check]; MP's outcome (flag seen, data stale) is forbidden under TSO and allowed under a relaxed model that may reorder accesses to different addresses, and a fence between the two accesses in each thread restores the sequentially consistent outcome sets of both tests [check]; two threads of m and n accesses have C(m + n, m) interleavings, 6 for SB and 20 for three accesses each [D, check]; a data-race-free program behaves sequentially consistently on any model that honours its synchronisation (the DRF-SC guarantee) [P, recalled]; LL/SC implements any read-modify-write and avoids the ABA problem of compare-and-swap because the store fails after any intervening write to the line [D]; a contended test-and-test-and-set lock costs O(P) bus transactions per release and about P(P + 1)/2 for P successive hand-offs (36 at P = 8), whereas a ticket lock needs one atomic operation per acquisition (its waiters still re-read the counter after each release) and an MCS lock causes O(1) traffic per hand-off because each waiter spins on its own flag [D, check]; a dissemination barrier needs ⌈log₂ P⌉ rounds, 6 at 64 and 7 at 100 threads [D, check]. Relation to distributed consistency: U14.15 owns hardware memory models and U9.16 owns distributed consistency (linearizability, CAP, quorums); sequential consistency is the hardware counterpart of Lamport's definition used in U9.16, TSO resembles a per-process ordered (FIFO) model, and fences play the role that synchronisation operations play in weak distributed models.

### T0929

Warp Scheduling, Divergence (Week 5): warps as the unit of scheduling, latency hiding by switching among resident warps, schedulers such as loose round-robin and greedy-then-oldest, occupancy and the resources that limit it (threads, blocks, registers, shared memory), branch divergence within a warp, the active mask, the reconvergence stack and immediate post-dominator reconvergence. GPU Architectures (the multicore course's Week 5): the GPU half of that week, the superscalar and multithreading half in U14.8.

Used by: avh, bwb, c6c, c6d, dfw, drd, fwi, gd4, l15, l1q, l1r, l5p, l66, l67, l8m, lf5, lgv, lsv, m1v, m51, mcp, mg0, my0, mzo, mzp, mzs, n3h, ok0, ozj, ozk, pnp, pus, q45, q4h, q4i, qwl, qyk, reg, riw, rkl

Multi-dimensional mapping of dataspace, Synchronization (Week 4): one-, two- and three-dimensional grids and blocks, mapping a thread to an element of a matrix or image, bounds checks for sizes that are not multiples of the block, grid-stride loops; `__syncthreads` within a block, why there is no barrier across blocks inside a kernel, atomic operations. Memory Access Coalescing (Week 6): how the loads of a warp are combined into 32-byte sectors and 128-byte lines, unit-stride versus strided and misaligned access, structure-of-arrays versus array-of-structures, shared-memory tiling and bank conflicts. Optimization examples : optimizing Reduction Kernels (Week 7): interleaved addressing with divergent branches, interleaved addressing with bank conflicts, sequential addressing, first add during load, unrolling the last warp, complete unrolling and multiple elements per thread (the classic sequence of seven versions, recalled, not checked). Optimization examples : Kernel Fusion, Thread and Block (Week 8): fusing element-wise kernels to remove intermediate global traffic, choosing block size and grid size, thread coarsening. Map of the GPU course's outline: the course covers basics of conventional CPU architectures (U14.5 to U14.9), their extensions for single instruction multiple data processing (SIMD) (U14.8) and finally the generalization of this concept in the form of single instruction multiple thread processing (SIMT) as is done in modern GPUs (U14.17); we cover GPU architecture basics in terms of functional units in U14.17 and then dive into the popular CUDA programming model commonly used for GPU programming here; in this context, architecture specific details like memory access coalescing, shared memory usage, GPU thread scheduling etc which primarily effect (source spelling) program performance are also covered in detail here and in U14.17; we next switch to a different SIMD programming language called OpenCL which can be used for programming both CPUs and GPUs in a generic manner in U14.19; the different architectureaware (source spelling) optimization techniques relevant to both CUDA and OpenCL run through U14.18 and U14.19; finally, where the outline says we provide the students with detail application development examples in two well-known GPU computing scenarios, those examples (efficient neural-network training and inference) are in U14.20.
